screens.title: Performance Optimization Fundamentals
screens.subtitle: Why stable frame rate, profiling, and targeted fixes matter for player experience

narration.text: Performance is not optional. Players notice stutters, hitches, and long load times even if a game’s mechanics are excellent. In this lesson we focus on practical, repeatable steps to find and fix bottlenecks: use the Unity Profiler to see whether your game is C P U-bound, G P U-bound, or suffering from frequent garbage collection; reduce draw calls with batching; avoid rendering unseen objects with effective culling; and prevent allocation spikes with object pooling. You will learn simple diagnostics, specific editor workflows, and code patterns you can apply immediately. For example, the Unity Profiler surfaces a clear Main Thread bar that tells you whether scripting or rendering work dominates a frame. Static batching reduces many small draw calls into fewer large ones when objects are stationary and share a material. Object pooling replaces repeated Instantiations and Destroy calls with reuse, smoothing memory behavior and preventing GC spikes. Over the next screens we’ll walk through profiler interpretation, batching choices, culling configuration, and an object pooling code example. Keep a small scene or a test build ready so you can profile as we go. By the end you’ll know how to find the next bottleneck and verify that your fix actually improved performance.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Profile first, fix only measured bottlenecks: use the Profiler, reduce draw calls with batching and culling, and avoid runtime allocations with object pooling.

Runtime

Pre-warm pools in Awake or Start.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll develop and how to verify them

narration.text: In this chapter you will acquire four practical skills you can use immediately. First, you will understand why performance matters: stable frame rate preserves control responsiveness and player immersion. For example, a mobile game that drops frames during explosions will feel laggy even if its mechanics are solid. Second, you'll learn to use the Unity Profiler to identify bottlenecks. The Profiler shows C P U and G P U bars and lets you drill into a single frame to find calls that dominate time. Third, you'll implement core optimization techniques: batching, culling, and object pooling. Each one targets a specific cost — draw calls, wasted rendering, and allocation overhead respectively. Finally, you'll distinguish between C P U-bound and G P U-bound problems and choose the right remedial action. A common mistake is treating every slowdown as a graphics issue; profiling shows whether the C P U or G P U is actually the limiting factor. Each objective is paired with a small milestone so you can validate competence: capture a profile, reduce draw calls, bake occlusion, and demonstrate pooling that avoids GC spikes.

keyIdea.title: What you'll prove
keyIdea.text: By the end you will measure a bottleneck with the Profiler, apply one targeted optimization, and verify measurable improvement.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice Milestones
screens.subtitle: How to verify each objective with a concrete task

narration.text: This second objectives screen turns each learning target into a verifiable practice task. First, to prove you understand why performance matters, run a simple scene and record how frame drops affect input responsiveness. Use that observation to prioritize one fix. Second, to prove profiler competency, capture a recorded profile and identify the top three contributors to frame time on the Main Thread. Practice drilling into a single frame and spotting the GarbageCollector spikes. Third, to demonstrate batching and culling, create a scene with many identical objects, measure draw calls, then apply static batching and record the reduced draw call count. Bake occlusion culling for a complex indoor scene and confirm fewer rendered objects. Fourth, to validate pooling skills, implement a pool for a rapid-fire projectile and show that GarbageCollector spikes disappear during intense firing. Each milestone is small, measurable, and repeatable. These practical checks turn abstract ideas into reliable developer habits.

screens.title: Why Performance Matters
screens.subtitle: How frame stability and load times affect player experience

narration.text: Performance is the backbone of player experience. When frame rate drops or load times spike, players perceive input lag, animation jitter, and game logic inconsistencies that break immersion. Define frame rate as the number of frames rendered per second; higher is smoother, but consistency matters even more than peak values. For example, a stable 30 frames per second with consistent frame time may feel better than a fluctuating 60 to 30 that creates visible stutter. Another practical example: two players test the same level where one device runs at steady 60 and another dips to 20 during particle-heavy scenes — the latter will experience delayed responses and missed collisions. A common misconception is that only graphics settings matter; often, scripting, physics, and allocation patterns cause C P U spikes that drop frame time regardless of visual fidelity. Key takeaway: always measure real device performance and prioritize fixes that remove the largest, repeatable sources of frame instability. Ask yourself: which single subsystem, when smoothed, would give the biggest consistent improvement to playability? Why Performance Matters means performance is about consistent frame times and responsive gameplay, not just raw frame-rate numbers.. In practical terms, how frame stability and load times affect player experience. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Performance is about consistent frame times and responsive gameplay, not just raw frame-rate numbers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Why Performance Matters
What is performance?
Consistent frame times, low load times, and predictable memory behavior that preserve control and immersion.
Example
A scene that drops from 60 to 15 FPS during explosions causes missed inputs and feels uncompetitive compared with steady 30 FPS.
Common misconception
High graphical settings are not always the cause; heavy scripting or frequent allocations can make the CPU the bottleneck.
Key Takeaway

Measure and target the dominant cause of instability; small fixes to the hot path produce the largest gains.

Why players notice it
  • Frame drops introduce input lag and break timing-critical mechanics.
  • Hitches caused by garbage collection interrupt animation and audio, creating abrupt pauses.
  • Load time delays increase churn and lower first-impression retention.
Reflection
Consider a game you played that stuttered. Was the issue sustained or episodic? That pattern suggests either a continuous bottleneck like too many draw calls, or an occasional allocation spike from repeated creation and destruction.

screens.title: The Unity Profiler — Read and Drill
screens.subtitle: How to capture frames and identify the hot path

narration.text: The Unity Profiler is the central tool for diagnosing runtime performance. At a high level, it records the time spent in C P U, G P U, Rendering, Physics, Memory and other modules while your game runs. To use it, open Window, Analysis, Profiler and start a recording session while running the scene. A useful process is: record baseline, reproduce the problematic action, stop recording, and then inspect the frame where the spike occurred. When you inspect a single frame, look for the heaviest bars on the Main Thread and expand them to see which functions or subsystems contribute most. For instance, if you see a large GarbageCollector spike, frequent allocations are the likely culprit. If the Rendering or G P U bars dominate, the problem is likely geometry, shader complexity, or overdraw. A concrete example: run a scene with many spawned objects and watch the Profiler while firing a rapid weapon — if the GC line spikes with destruction events, converting to pooling will remove that spike. A common error is assuming the highest C P U usage component is the cause; instead, look for sudden spikes or repeated heavy calls that align with gameplay events. Try capturing before-and-after profiles to verify your fixes.

keyIdea.title: Profiler process
keyIdea.text: Record a session, reproduce the issue, drill into the offending frame, and inspect the Main Thread and Memory modules to find the hot functions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › The Unity Profiler — Read and Drill
Profiling workflow
  1. Open Profiler: Window > Analysis > Profiler and enable recording.
  2. Run the scene and reproduce the problematic action to record the spike.
  3. Pause or stop recording, then select the frame with the spike to inspect details.
  4. Expand Main Thread and Memory to find the functions or allocations responsible.
Example
In a test where bullets are created rapidly, record firing and inspect the GarbageCollector graph to see allocation spikes caused by Instantiate/Destroy.
Key Takeaway

Use frame-by-frame analysis to connect a visible spike to specific calls or systems before applying fixes.

Supporting notes
  • CPU-bound: high Main Thread usage. Look at scripting, physics, and draw call submission.
  • GPU-bound: high GPU or Rendering bars. Investigate shaders, vertex count, and overdraw.
  • Memory issues: watch the Memory and GC allocations to find frequent allocations and deallocations.
Common mistake
Fixing visuals before profiling can waste effort. Start with a profile and verify the subsystem that actually needs work.

screens.title: CPU-bound vs GPU-bound
screens.subtitle: How to tell which subsystem is limiting your frame rate

narration.text: Distinguishing C P U-bound from G P U-bound frames is essential because the remedies differ. Claim: a C P U-bound game is limited by the processor preparing draw calls, updating scripts, and running physics; a G P U-bound game is limited by the graphics hardware rendering vertices and pixels. Concrete example: if the Profiler shows a high Main Thread bar while G P U usage is low, you are C P U-bound — reducing draw calls via batching or optimizing scripts will help. Conversely, if Rendering or G P U bars are high, reducing shader complexity, polygon counts, or screen resolution will help. A useful misconception to check is assuming that reducing shader quality always helps a C P U-bound problem — it may not, because the C P U cost of submitting many draw calls remains. Another contrast: garbage collection shows up under Memory and can cause short but severe hitches regardless of whether C P U or G P U is the steady limiter. Closing takeaway: use profiler bars, per-frame details, and reproducible tests to decide the appropriate optimization strategy rather than guessing based on visual symptoms.

keyIdea.title: Diagnostic rule
keyIdea.text: If the Main Thread dominates, consider batching and script/physics work; if GPU/Rendering dominates, optimize shaders, geometry, and overdraw.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › CPU-bound vs GPU-bound
CPU-bound
High Main Thread usage from scripting, physics, or many draw calls submitted by the CPU.
Symptoms: High Main Thread bar, low GPU usage, frame time dominated by script or rendering submission.
Fixes: Reduce draw calls (batching), optimize scripts, cache components, reduce expensive physics checks.
Misconception: Lowering shader quality won’t help a CPU-bound issue caused by excessive draw calls.
GPU-bound
High Rendering or GPU bars, often caused by heavy shaders, high triangle counts, or large overdraw.
Symptoms: GPU bar is the limiting factor; reducing polycount or shader complexity lowers frame time.
Fixes: Optimize shaders, reduce polygons, enable occlusion culling or lower render resolution.
Tip: Use a GPU profiler when available for per-pass shader costs; in the Editor, Rendering and GPU bars help narrow the cause.
Quick diagnostic checklist
Check Main Thread
Check Rendering/GPU
Check Memory/GC

screens.title: Draw Calls and Batching
screens.subtitle: How draw calls cost CPU time and when to use static vs dynamic batching

narration.text: A draw call is the instruction the C P U sends to the G P U to render a group of triangles. Each draw call has C P U-side overhead for state changes and submission. When many small objects use separate draw calls, the C P U becomes busy preparing each call and your game can become C P U-bound. Unity reduces this cost with batching, which combines meshes or draw submissions. Static batching merges meshes at build time for objects marked as Static that share the same material; it is excellent for stationary geometry and produces large savings with minimal runtime cost. Dynamic batching works at runtime for small moving objects that share a material but requires strict limits on vertex counts and object transforms. A concrete example: 1,000 identical cubes using the same material and marked Static will be combined into fewer draw calls and dramatically reduce C P U work when the camera looks at them. A common mistake is marking animated or frequently moving objects as Static; this prevents movement and breaks batching assumptions. Key takeaway: choose static batching for stationary geometry, and rely on dynamic batching only for small, moveable objects that meet Unity’s limits.

keyIdea.title: Draw calls
keyIdea.text: Minimize draw calls with static batching for stationary objects and dynamic batching only for small, moving objects sharing materials.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Draw Calls and Batching
What is a draw call?
An instruction from CPU to GPU to render a set of triangles. Each call has overhead on the CPU side.
Static batching: Combine stationary meshes sharing a material at build time. Best for level geometry.
Dynamic batching: Runtime combination for small moving objects that meet vertex and transform constraints.
Common mistake: Marking animated objects as Static — doing so prevents movement and can break gameplay.
Concrete example
Spawn 1,000 identical cubes with the same material. Without batching, CPU must issue many draw calls. With static batching, Unity merges meshes and reduces draw calls substantially, lowering CPU time on the Main Thread.
Key Takeaway
Batching reduces CPU overhead. Use static for stationary objects and dynamic only when objects are small and moving.

screens.title: Static Batching in Practice
screens.subtitle: Marking objects static, shared materials and verifying results

narration.text: Static batching is most effective when many stationary objects share the same material. The practical process is: ensure identical materials, mark objects as Static in the Inspector or via script, and then rebuild or run the scene to let Unity combine meshes. A concrete workflow: create a grid of identical meshes, assign the same Material asset, and set their isStatic flag to true. Then profile the scene: you should see fewer draw calls and reduced C P U submission time. If the material differs per object, batching cannot combine them. A common mistake is using different material instances for objects that visually appear identical; confirm they reference the same Material asset. If your scene uses lightmapping or other static data, enabling Static may also trigger other bake steps — account for those in build time. Key takeaway: static batching can yield large gains for level geometry, but verify that objects truly do not need to move before marking them Static. After batching, always capture a new profile to measure the real impact. Static Batching in Practice means use the same material, mark as static, and reprofile to confirm draw call reductions before and after enabling static batching.. In practical terms, marking objects static, shared materials and verifying results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical steps
keyIdea.text: Use the same Material, mark as Static, and reprofile to confirm draw call reductions before and after enabling static batching.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Static Batching in Practice
Step-by-step
  1. Make sure objects share the exact same Material asset.
  2. Mark objects as Static in the Inspector or set newCube.isStatic = true in code.
  3. Run the scene and measure draw calls in the Profiler before and after.
Example verification
Before: 1,000 draw calls. After: significantly fewer draw calls and lower Main Thread time for rendering submission.
Caveats
  • Static batching increases build time and memory for combined meshes.
  • Animated or moving objects cannot be static; doing so will break motion.
  • Materials must be identical references; duplicated instances prevent batching.
Key Takeaway

Static batching pays off for stationary, material-shared geometry. Confirm the material references and reprofile to measure benefit.

screens.title: Culling Techniques
screens.subtitle: Frustum culling vs occlusion culling and when each helps

narration.text: Culling prevents the renderer from drawing objects that don't contribute to the current view. Frustum culling is automatic in Unity: objects outside the camera’s view frustum are skipped. This is fundamental but only helps if objects are truly off-screen. Occlusion culling goes further by skipping objects that are within the frustum but hidden behind other occluders, like walls in an indoor scene. To use occlusion culling, bake an occlusion dataset via Window, Rendering, Occlusion Culling and test playback. A concrete example: in a corridor-based level, frustum culling still considers objects beyond a doorway if they are within the frustum, but occlusion culling will avoid rendering enemies behind closed doors, greatly reducing polygon processing. A common misconception is that occlusion culling always improves performance; in very open scenes with few occluders, the bake overhead and runtime checks may not be worth it. Key takeaway: use frustum culling by default and employ occlusion culling in complex occlusion-rich environments to significantly reduce G P U workload. Culling Techniques means use frustum culling automatically and add occlusion culling for complex environments where many objects are hidden behind occluders.. In practical terms, frustum culling vs occlusion culling and when each helps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Culling summary
keyIdea.text: Use frustum culling automatically and add occlusion culling for complex environments where many objects are hidden behind occluders.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Culling Techniques
Frustum Culling
Built-in: objects outside camera frustum are not rendered.
This handles simple off-screen geometry automatically and requires no setup, but it cannot skip objects that are within the frustum but occluded behind other geometry.
Example
A distant mountain outside the camera frustum is ignored by frustum culling.
Occlusion Culling
Configured and baked: prevents rendering of objects hidden behind occluders even if inside the frustum.
Use when scenes have many hidden objects, like indoor levels with walls and closed doors. Bake occlusion data in the editor and test to confirm runtime savings.
Key Takeaway

Occlusion culling is powerful in occlusion-rich scenes but offers little benefit in open worlds. Always measure after baking.

screens.title: Object Pooling — Pattern and Practice
screens.subtitle: Avoid GC spikes by reusing instances instead of frequent Instantiate/Destroy

narration.text: Object pooling is a simple but powerful pattern: pre-instantiate a set of objects and reuse them instead of creating and destroying instances at runtime. This avoids frequent memory allocation and deallocation that leads to GarbageCollector spikes and visible hitches. Practical implementation involves creating a manager or singleton pool that holds inactive objects in a queue, provides a GetPooledObject method to activate and hand out an instance, and a ReturnPooledObject method to deactivate and enqueue it for future reuse. For example, instead of instantiating a bullet on each shot, fetch one from the pool and activate it. If the pool runs out, you can either expand it or log a warning and consider increasing initial size. A common misconception is that pooling is only for projectiles; actually, pooling helps for any frequently created short-lived objects such as particle effects, temporary UI elements, or enemy spawns. Key takeaway: pool during Start or Awake, avoid Destroy calls on frequently used objects, and reprofile to confirm GC reduction. The next visual contains a code example that follows these best practices. Object Pooling — Pattern and Practice means pre-instantiate a pool of objects, activate on get, deactivate and return on release to prevent runtime allocations and gc spikes.. In practical terms, avoid gc spikes by reusing instances instead of frequent instantiate/destroy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pooling pattern
keyIdea.text: Pre-instantiate a pool of objects, activate on Get, deactivate and return on Release to prevent runtime allocations and GC spikes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Object Pooling — Pattern and Practice
Core implementation
A singleton pool that pre-instantiates objects and serves them on request prevents allocations during gameplay.
C# example
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;

public class ObjectPool : MonoBehaviour
{
    public static ObjectPool Instance { get; private set; }

    [SerializeField] private GameObject prefab;
    [SerializeField] private int initialPoolSize = 10;

    private Queue<GameObject> pool = new Queue<GameObject>();

    void Awake()
    {
        if (Instance == null) Instance = this; else Destroy(gameObject);

        for (int i = 0; i < initialPoolSize; i++)
        {
            GameObject obj = Instantiate(prefab);
            obj.SetActive(false);
            pool.Enqueue(obj);
        }
    }

    public GameObject GetPooledObject()
    {
        if (pool.Count > 0)
        {
            GameObject obj = pool.Dequeue();
            obj.SetActive(true);
            return obj;
        }
        else
        {
            GameObject obj = Instantiate(prefab);
            Debug.LogWarning("Object pool expanded at runtime. Consider increasing initialPoolSize.");
            return obj;
        }
    }

    public void ReturnPooledObject(GameObject obj)
    {
        obj.SetActive(false);
        pool.Enqueue(obj);
    }
}
Key Takeaway

Pool frequently spawned, short-lived objects to avoid runtime allocation and visible GC hitches.

Usage example
Call ObjectPool.Instance.GetPooledObject() instead of Instantiate, and ObjectPool.Instance.ReturnPooledObject(myObj) instead of Destroy. Pre-warm the pool to expected peak concurrency to avoid runtime expansion.
Common mistake
Not caching references or repeatedly calling GetComponent in Update loops — cache components and reuse references to reduce CPU cost.

screens.title: Spawner Example Before Pooling
screens.subtitle: A starter script that creates many objects and why it causes issues

narration.text: This example demonstrates a common anti-pattern: instantiating hundreds of objects at Start or during gameplay without reuse. The provided ManyCubesSpawner script creates a large number of cubes in a grid or random pattern to simulate an unoptimized scene. When you run it, observe the Profiler: the number of draw calls is high and the Main Thread shows increased submission time. If this spawner uses Instantiate for each cube and later destroys them frequently, memory allocations cause GarbageCollector activity. Concrete example: spawn 500 to 1000 cubes at Start with individual material instances — this prevents static batching and increases draw calls. A misconception is thinking that simply reducing the number of objects is the only solution; in many cases you can keep object counts but rearrange materials and batching, or use pooling to reduce allocation cost. In practice, start by profiling the unoptimized scene, apply static batching and pooling as appropriate, and then capture an after profile to verify the improvement. The code block shown here is the baseline you should test first so you can measure real gains from optimizations.

keyIdea.title: Before optimization
keyIdea.text: Instantiating many objects without batching or pooling increases draw calls and memory churn; profile this baseline to measure improvements.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Spawner Example Before Pooling
Starter spawner code
using UnityEngine;

public class ManyCubesSpawner : MonoBehaviour
{
    public GameObject cubePrefab;
    public int cubeCount = 500;
    public float spawnRange = 50f;

    void Start()
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < cubeCount; i++)
        {
            Vector3 randomPos = new Vector3(
                Random.Range(-spawnRange, spawnRange),
                0,
                Random.Range(-spawnRange, spawnRange)
            );
            GameObject newCube = Instantiate(cubePrefab, randomPos, Quaternion.identity);
            // Optionally mark as static for static batching:
            // newCube.isStatic = true; 
        }
    }
}
Why this is costly
Each Instantiate call allocates memory and causes CPU work to set up transforms and renderers. Without shared material references and static flags, draw calls remain high. Repeated creation and destruction also produces GC allocations.
Common mistake
Leaving unique material instances on visually identical objects prevents batching. Always reuse Material assets for identical objects.
Key Takeaway

Profile the baseline and then apply batching/pooling to measure real improvements.

screens.title: Hands-on: Optimize a Cube Scene
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step lab using static batching and object pooling

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks through optimizing a scene populated by many identical objects. Next, create a script that instantiates 500 to 1,000 cubes in a random grid pattern at Start and run the scene while recording a baseline profile. Observe draw calls and Main Thread cost. Step two: enable static batching by marking the cubes as Static in the Inspector or set newCube. isStatic = true in your script, ensuring they share the same Material asset. Rerun the scene and compare profiles to see draw call and C P U reductions. Step three: implement an ObjectPool for dynamic cases or replace Instantiate in your spawner with ObjectPool. Instance. GetPooledObject and ReturnPooledObject. Reproduce the same activity and check the Memory and GarbageCollector graphs to confirm reduced allocation spikes. Common mistake: forgetting to warm the pool before gameplay so the pool expands at runtime and still causes allocations. Key takeaway: always verify the effect of a change with before/after profiles. In practical terms, a step-by-step lab using static batching and object pooling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Create baseline, apply static batching, implement pooling, and compare profiles to confirm reduced draw calls and GC spikes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Hands-on: Optimize a Cube Scene
Step 1 — Baseline
Create cube prefab, spawn 500–1,000 instances, run and record a profile. Note draw calls, Main Thread, and GC spikes.
Step 2 — Static batching
Ensure the same Material, mark objects Static or set isStatic in code, then rerun and compare draw calls.
Step 3 — Object pooling
Replace Instantiate/Destroy with GetPooledObject and ReturnPooledObject. Pre-warm the pool to expected peak.
Common mistakes & checks
  • Not sharing Material references prevents batching.
  • Expanding pools at runtime creates allocations; pre-warm pools for steady performance.
  • For occlusion culling, remember to bake and test; it won’t help open outdoor scenes much.
Key Takeaway

Measure first, make one targeted change, then re-measure to confirm the impact; repeat until performance goals are met.

screens.title: Profiling Workflow and Common Mistakes
screens.subtitle: Iterative profiling, targeted fixes, and pitfalls to avoid

narration.text: Optimization is iterative: profile, fix, and re-profile. Start by capturing a baseline profile under realistic conditions. Identify the dominant subsystem and select a targeted fix — batching for many small draw calls, occlusion culling for hidden geometry, pooling for allocation spikes, or shader/mesh simplification for G P U time. After implementing a change, capture another profile and compare metrics rather than relying on subjective feel. Common mistakes include: optimizing graphics without profiling, which may not address C P U-side bottlenecks; not sharing materials which prevents batching; calling GetComponent repeatedly in update loops instead of caching references; and failing to warm pools so they expand during gameplay. A concrete example: you fix a perceived G P U problem by reducing texture quality but the Main Thread is still high due to excessive draw calls; your profile shows the real issue. Final takeaway: adopt small, measurable iterations and keep the Profiler as part of your development loop to prevent regressions as features are added. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Profiling Workflow and Common Mistakes
Iterative checklist
  1. Record a baseline profile under realistic gameplay conditions.
  2. Identify the dominant subsystem or repeated spike causing visible hitches.
  3. Apply a single targeted fix and collect a new profile for comparison.
  4. Repeat until the performance target is reached.
Pitfalls to avoid
  • Optimizing without profiling and fixing areas that aren’t the bottleneck.
  • Not sharing material references, which blocks batching opportunities.
  • Calling GetComponent in Update without caching results.
  • Letting pools expand at runtime instead of pre-warming to expected peak.
Key Takeaway

Use small, measurable optimizations guided by profiler data and bake verification into your workflow.

screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let’s summarize the essential points. First, profile before you optimize: the Unity Profiler shows C P U, G P U, Memory and other modules so you can find the true bottleneck. Second, distinguish C P U-bound from G P U-bound problems: high Main Thread suggests C P U work like draw call submission or scripting; high Rendering/G P U bars point to shader or geometry costs. Third, minimize draw calls with batching: use static batching for stationary objects that share a material and dynamic batching only for small movable objects. Fourth, use culling to avoid rendering unseen geometry: frustum culling is automatic, and occlusion culling helps in occluder-rich scenes. Fifth, use object pooling to avoid frequent allocations and GC spikes by reusing instances. Practice the lab workflow: baseline, change one thing, reprofile, and measure. Keep the Profiler in your daily workflow to catch regressions early. Which technique would make the largest difference in your current project?
